technique: verbs over adjectives — how the action words carry the weight
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: verbs. A verb is an action word. It tells you what something does.

This poem leans on its verbs to do the work. "The boots stand by the door where you stepped out of them." Stand and stepped. Both are plain actions, and they tell you more than a long description of the boots would. "Pull the laces slow." Pull is a thing you do with your hands. "it asks one thing, and the one thing can be done." Asks, done.

Here is why it works on a listener. A verb makes you see a body move. You picture the stepping, the pulling. That is clearer than being told the boots were tired or dirty.

Try this: take one line from your draft and cut every describing word. Keep only the action. See if the line still stands.

The second time through, listen for how the verbs push toward the last line, "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
The boots stand by the door where you stepped out of them,
one tipped against the other, mud gone stiff and gray,
holding the shape of the day they walked through—
a thing you didn't finish, laid down whole for morning.
There's always that: the ledger of small debts,
a tally in the head that keeps its own cold count,
names you turned over past the hour you meant to sleep.
Let them keep. The kettle's business now is water,
and the window's gone from black to the dull pewter
that means the hills are out there, waiting on their edges.
Pull the laces slow. The cold's honest, at least—
it asks one thing, and the one thing can be done.

There's a long patch of ordered work waiting, and it goes easier with the first light behind it—

So — up!
